items.t: US stocks rally and dollar slides as investors weigh Democratic midterm wins
items.s: US shares rallied on Wednesday and the dollar weakened as investors weighed Democratic gains in the midterm elections, which were seen as a possible brake on Donald Trump’s policymaking. Government bond yields also fell as fears about the economic impact eased.
p: US equities climbed as investors assessed the Democratic takeover of the Senate and the House of Representatives. According to the Guardian, the Dow Jones gained about 2%, while the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 each rose by more than 1%. The advance erased overnight losses in US stock futures that had followed the election news.

The dollar weakened against the currencies of America’s main trading partners and fell to a one-month low. Its index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of six currencies, reached its lowest level in a month. The pound climbed to its strongest point since mid-September and the euro also gained. The dollar lost ground against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders typically buy in uncertain times.

Investors moved into US Treasuries, which are seen as a shelter from the political gridlock expected for the remainder of Trump’s term. The yield on the 10-year bond dropped 4.7 basis points to 4.918%, while the two-year yield fell 3.7 basis points to 4.597%. Yields move inversely to bond prices, so falling yields mean prices rose.

The Guardian reports that voters across the country rejected Trump and the Republican agenda, with Democrats winning Senate seats in long-standing Republican strongholds including Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina. Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said the scale of the defeats would raise doubts about Trump’s capacity to pass his agenda over the next two years. Gold and silver attracted buyers as safe havens, and gold rose 2.2%, topping $4,000 an ounce.

European markets also rose in early trading. London’s FTSE 100 gained 0.2%, Germany’s Dax added almost 0.6%, France’s Cac 40 rose 0.4% and Italy’s FTSE MiB jumped almost 1.4%. Bank shares rose 2.8%. Clean energy companies, which have borne much of the impact of Trump’s policies, were also among the strongest performers, with Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems up nearly 5% and Ørsted up 7.4%.

Technology stocks told a different story. Shares tied to the sector fell in Asian trading on expectations that Democrats would push for tighter regulation. Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said SpaceX was down 5% in premarket trading and Tesla was lower by more than 4%. She linked the moves to the prospect of closer scrutiny of technology firms, which could also cast doubt on a possible merger of Elon Musk’s two companies. Musk, the world’s richest person, had put $446m (£331m) into the midterms through Republican-aligned political action committees and groups, and Brooks said most Democrats regard him negatively.

Chris Turner, global head of markets at ING, pointed to Gina Hinojosa’s victory in the Texas governor’s race, which he said was won on a promise of an immediate moratorium on data-centre construction. He said speculation that a Democratic Congress could slow spending on the sector had briefly weighed on markets. Jesper Koll of Monex Group argued that momentum in the sector had turned negative regardless of which party held a majority. Tai Hui of JP Morgan Asset Management noted that Trump could still shape markets through trade and tariffs, foreign policy and existing regulations, and some analysts doubt the result will change US policy much given his reliance on executive orders.
items.cav: Much of the market reasoning rests on analysts’ expectations about a Democratic Congress and tighter tech regulation, not on any announced policy. The Texas moratorium pledge is described second-hand by ING, and the Musk merger doubts are XTB’s interpretation. The report gives no closing figures for the day’s US indices.
items.op: Markets are pricing in a more constrained president, but a constrained president is not the same as an accountable one. Investors should not be the only ones judging whether checks on executive power work. Congress should use its oversight role openly, with clear rules for tech firms and transparency over large political donations.

items.t: Burnham says US midterm results offer the world a chance to focus on cost of living and the Iran war
items.s: The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections could give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing living costs. He made the remarks in an interview at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua.
p: Asked whether he worried that the results might make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham said the US president had accepted the outcome. He said he believed the world now had a chance to unite around cost of living pressures, which affect people everywhere.

Burnham said that he had made the cost of living his central priority in his first three months in Downing Street and that the government had taken steps on it. He argued, however, that prices would not fall while the conflict in the Middle East remained unresolved. He also referred to the war in Ukraine, which he said Russia had started.

Some politicians and commentators have read the results as a sign that rightwing populism is in retreat across the world. Burnham stopped short of endorsing that broader view. He said instead that voters in the United States appeared to want the world’s leaders to come together on issues that matter to ordinary people.

He said countries could not tackle cost of living problems alone and would struggle while nations remained divided. Burnham described a new approach in the Middle East, which he linked to recent announcements by the foreign secretary on sanctions over Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. He also pointed to a new approach towards Europe and to renewed engagement with the Commonwealth.

On the Iran war, Burnham said he would work for de-escalation. He set out a clear aim: a resolution to the conflict and the Strait of Hormuz fully reopened. He said he would press that message in calls with other leaders.
The Guardian’s live coverage of the interview was introduced by Louise Haigh, who was standing in for Burnham. The coverage also noted that the country would observe Remembrance Sunday that weekend.

The reporting relies on Burnham’s own interview remarks and the live blog’s summary. It does not set out the detailed results of the US elections or independent assessments of how the diplomacy would work in practice.
items.cav: The account rests on Burnham’s own remarks in one interview, so his claims about the US results and diplomacy are his, not independently verified. The sources do not say which politicians or commentators read the results as a retreat of populism, and they give no detail on the specific sanctions or on how the proposed talks would proceed.
items.op: Leaders who benefit from a rival’s electoral setback should not treat cost of living relief and an end to war as a bargaining chip. Public accountability means saying plainly which diplomatic steps are being taken and who is taking them. Britain’s prime minister has set an agenda; the test is whether his words on Hormuz and the Middle East turn into verifiable action.

items.t: Hackers Tampered With Freezers Storing Blood in France as Attribution Remains Unclear
items.s: French authorities say cold storage used for blood donations was hit by recent cyber-attacks, while researchers chase competing theories about who was responsible. Officials report no health impact so far.
p: French authorities say that refrigeration units at medical facilities used to store donated blood were affected by recent cyber-attacks carried out by unknown hackers. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms holding blood were affected and temperatures were set to rise, but staff stepped in to protect the supplies.

The EFS said that “no health impact has been identified” and that no loss of blood products was to be reported. Until now, the attacks had been linked publicly only to supermarkets across Europe, so the reported impact on blood storage marks a broader target set.

Online rumours have pointed to Russian hacktivist groups. Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted claims that they had breached Danfoss, a equipment maker, which fuelled speculation that they were behind the freezer intrusions. Analysts have since questioned whether that claim shows any link to the supermarket attacks. Experts also say Iranian hacktivists, state-backed hackers or even teenagers playing pranks cannot be ruled out.

Several cyber-security firms have set up honeypots, which are decoy systems designed to look like vulnerable freezer software so that attackers reveal their methods. Previdian, a Spanish company, said the second wave, which hit several European countries at once, appeared highly targeted. Its researcher Ryan Dewhurst argued that the simultaneous hits and the overnight timing of temperature increases suggest planning and coordination. He added that the entry point was not hard to exploit, since the products were poorly protected and known methods were already circulating.

Lupovis, a firm based in Strathclyde, reported that its decoys, placed in several parts of the world, began drawing activity about ten days before the second wave. Its founder, Dr Xavier Bellekens, said that the scanning and probing targeted only European sites, with none of the decoys in places such as Africa or South America attacked.

Sekoia, a French cyber-defence firm, also saw scanning before the second wave but said it might have been automated and not malicious. Its report said the activity was consistent with Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, but it also pointed to Iranian state-linked actors. It noted that about 40 Israeli supermarkets using Danfoss controllers were compromised in 2022. A Sekoia spokesperson later told the BBC that the company had “no technical evidence” of involvement by Russian-speaking groups.

Separately, freezers at at least six US military bases were reportedly forced into defrost mode in late August, similar to the French incidents. The controller models involved have not been confirmed, and investigations are ongoing.
items.cav: Attribution is unresolved. The Russian and Iranian theories rest on hacker claims, analyst speculation and a firm's broader findings, and the sources do not confirm which controller models were used in France or the US. The EFS statement on health impact is the organisation's own account.
items.op: When life-saving medical supplies are put at risk, the public deserves clear answers about what was hit and who is responsible. Rumours and unverified hacker boasts should not stand in for evidence. Authorities should publish what they know about the affected equipment and the timeline, and fast.

items.t: Democrats’ House and Senate wins open a new phase of oversight of Trump
items.s: Democrats have taken control of the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms, according to The Guardian, giving them tools to investigate the administration and slow its appointments. The paper sets out which investigations they are likely to pursue first.
p: Democrats have flipped both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, a result The Guardian describes as a major rebuke of Republicans and of Donald Trump’s agenda. With majorities in both the House and Senate, the last two years of Trump’s presidency are expected to look very different from the first half.

The House win came after a series of victories in Republican-held districts pushed Democrats past the 218-seat threshold needed for a majority. The paper reports that Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become majority leader, and that Republicans will no longer be able to pass legislation through the chamber without Democratic support.

A Democratic majority could launch investigations, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained scrutiny. The Senate, meanwhile, confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, so a Democratic majority could block or delay many appointments and push the White House into negotiations over legislation.

The Guardian names several possible early targets. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has put Trump family corruption at the top of his list. Representative Jamie Raskin has asked for information on the business dealings of Jared Kushner and Donald Trump Jr.

The paper also points to the Epstein files. It says the Justice Department missed a legal deadline to disclose them, released about 3.5 million of the roughly 6 million pages it held, and said the rest were duplicates. Heavy redactions and the apparent accidental disclosure of victims’ names have drawn bipartisan concern, and the department faces a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang.

Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports that defence money was steered toward companies linked to the Trump family. Those reports are cited by Crow, and the article does not independently verify them.

On impeachment, Jeffries has said Democrats have ruled nothing out, while the current House majority leader, Steve Scalise, has predicted an attempt on “Day 1”. The article recalls that after Democrats flipped the House in 2018, the House voted mostly on party lines to impeach Trump just over a year after the midterms. He was acquitted by the Republican-controlled Senate. He was impeached and acquitted again in 2021 over the January 6 attack on the Capitol.
items.cav: The source is a Guardian explainer based on reporting about intentions, not completed actions; no investigation has yet been launched in the article. The Scalise prediction and the Pentagon claims are attributed to the people quoted, and the Justice Department’s duplicate explanation is its own account.
items.op: Oversight is the least glamorous power a majority holds, and often the most useful for voters who want to know how their government works. The Epstein file handling shows why: missed deadlines, withheld pages and exposed victims’ names are transparency failures that should be pursued whichever party holds the gavel. Democrats should apply that standard to the White House with the same rigour they demand of others.

items.t: Kellogg’s admits Rice Krispies’ snap, crackle and pop may be quieter after recipe change backlash
items.s: Kellogg’s has told the BBC that the sound Rice Krispies makes in milk may now be softer and slower to appear, after online anger over a reformulation. The firm links the switch to weather-related supply problems.
p: Kellogg’s has acknowledged to the BBC that the noise Rice Krispies makes when milk is added may now be softer and slower to arrive. The admission follows a wave of complaints about the reformulated cereal, which the company says was prompted by pressures on its supply chain.
According to the BBC’s report, Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer made from whole rice grains. Instead, the toasted puffs are produced with a blend of corn flour and rice flour.

A Kellogg’s spokesperson said preserving the famous sound had been a major priority in developing the new recipe. The firm was answering online criticism that the taste had shifted and that some fans missed the crisp noise they had long associated with the brand.

Some shoppers said their children had stopped eating the cereals. A parent called Dani posted on TikTok that the new version lacked the characteristic crackle and that her toddler refused it. Another user, Lauren, said she had eaten Rice Krispies at breakfast for years and could tell the difference straight away once milk was poured in.

The company said the revised products had been tested for flavour, look and mouthfeel. It blamed shifting weather patterns for disrupting supplies of certain grains and cereals, and argued that the changes would keep quality steady while extreme weather pushes up ingredient costs.

Kellogg’s also pointed to extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023, which it said had reduced the availability of rice varieties it uses in breakfast cereals. It stressed that the products contain no artificial colourings, flavourings or sweeteners, and that their fibre, vitamin D and iron content remains the same.

The packaging will now carry a warning that the product contains wheat gluten. The earlier labels said the products “may contain gluten”, reflecting the risk of cross-contamination in a factory that handles other cereals.

The BBC noted that recipe changes are a constant headache for large food brands. Chocolate makers have repeatedly faced accusations of cutting cocoa, and when the Scottish soft drink Irn Bru reduced its sugar in 2018, fans stocked up on the original. Kellogg’s cereals have been reformulated before too, with salt reduced in the 1990s and sugar lowered in 2018.

The wider context is El Niño, which has brought droughts, floods and heatwaves to many regions this year. South East Asia grows more than a quarter of the world’s rice, and the World Meteorological Agency expects the event to persist until at least 2027, adding to pressure on food manufacturers.
items.cav: The complaints about sound and taste rest largely on social media posts and the experiences of a few shoppers, not on measured tests. The link to El Niño is the company’s own explanation, and the sources do not say how much the change has raised costs.
items.op: Companies that quietly reformulate much-loved products owe customers clear disclosure, not reassurance after the backlash. The gluten labelling change shows that openness is possible. Kellogg’s should have explained the trade-offs before shoppers noticed them on the tongue.

items.t: Zelensky awards Melania Trump Ukraine’s top women’s honour after Oleshky ceasefire
items.s: Ukraine’s president has given Melania Trump the Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, after a truce let hundreds of people leave the occupied city of Oleshky. Russian and Ukrainian delegations are due at the White House on Thursday at her invitation.
p: Volodymyr Zelensky has bestowed Ukraine’s most prestigious decoration for women on US First Lady Melania Trump. A presidential decree says the award honours her personal role in aiding Ukraine through humanitarian channels, and it cites her broader relief efforts, including work on behalf of Ukrainian children caught up in the conflict.

The honour comes shortly after a pause in fighting in Kherson, in southern Ukraine, which made it possible to move several hundred civilians out of Oleshky, a city under Russian occupation. Those evacuations are the main reason the truce is being discussed in the context of Melania Trump.

Delegations from both countries, consisting of human rights ombudsmen who worked on the evacuation and senior government figures, are scheduled to convene at the White House on Thursday. The White House says Melania Trump “independently initiated engagement” between the two warring countries and helped secure the truce, describing it as a first of its kind for an American first lady. Moscow and Kyiv have both credited her with brokering the arrangement, yet neither has spelled out what her involvement amounted to.

On the Ukrainian side, the group includes ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and parliamentarian Davyd Arakhamia, who has earlier sat on Kyiv’s negotiating team in peace talks with Moscow. Russia’s delegation, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, will include ombudsman Yana Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a businessman with close ties to the Kremlin who has often joined US-mediated ceasefire discussions. Lubinets and Lantratova entered Oleshky together the previous week, an unusual display of joint work between the two governments.

The agenda for the White House meeting has not been released. Melania Trump is also expected to address the Oleshky truce publicly on Thursday, according to the White House website. Separately, officials from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are set to gather in Abu Dhabi next week, the first three-way session since February. US envoy Steve Witkoff said those discussions would centre on security arrangements for after the war and on lowering tensions.

Melania Trump has generally kept her distance from diplomacy. In 2025, however, she said that a line of contact with Russian President Vladimir Putin had been set up and had helped reunite displaced Ukrainian children with their families. Kyiv puts the number of children taken to Russia and Belarus since 2022 at nearly 20,000, and the United Nations has earlier this year labelled such transfers a crime against humanity and a war crime.
items.cav: The sources do not explain what Melania Trump actually did to secure the truce, and the thanks from Moscow and Kyiv come without detail. The White House’s account is its own claim, and the agenda for Thursday’s meeting has not been published.
items.op: Honours and praise cost little when the mechanism of a deal stays hidden. If a First Lady is credited with brokering a ceasefire, the public deserves to know what she did, who else was involved, and what the Thursday talks will decide. Ceasefires that save civilians should be judged on transparent terms.

items.t: Democrats’ midterm win could make a weakened Trump less predictable abroad, Europeans fear
items.s: Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory leaves Donald Trump politically weakened in the final stretch of his presidency. Some European officials fear that could make him harder to predict abroad, according to Euronews.
p: Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress and won governorships in several states, a result Euronews frames as a heavy setback for Republicans and for a president who was not himself on the ballot. Trump now has roughly two years left in office, and the outcome has been read as a judgement on his unpopular administration.

Euronews reports that an EU diplomat expects Trump to lean more heavily on foreign policy, an area where he can act with less interference from Congress. The diplomat described him as likely to be more dangerous than a leader simply running out his term. Italian MEP Brando Benifei, who chairs the European Parliament’s delegation for relations with the US, warned that a more erratic approach could bring added trouble for Europe over Ukraine and the Middle East.

Iran is among the most pressing concerns for European officials. According to the report, fighting that started on 28 February has left the Strait of Hormuz largely closed, with only a brief opening in June, and the resulting shipping limits keep energy costs high. Romanian MEP Virgil-Daniel Popescu argued that the elections alone will not lower prices, and that what matters is whether Washington and Tehran pursue de-escalation. Dimitar Likov of the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies doubts this will happen soon.

Congress holds the constitutional authority to declare war and can pass measures seeking to end American military involvement. Trump could veto such a measure, and overriding him would require two-thirds majorities in both chambers, a high bar even after the Democratic gains. Trump has downplayed the chance of further strikes on Iran while maintaining that US forces stay ready to act if needed.

On Ukraine, the report says ties between Washington and Kyiv have worsened, with Trump criticised for permitting Russian diesel imports and easing sanctions on Moscow. A Democratic Congress is expected to push for continued supplies of air defence systems and missile interceptors, though the Senate filibuster and Trump’s veto power constrain it. Zelenskyy has not publicly responded to the results, and Russia said it hoped the vote would not disrupt Trump’s push for a settlement it describes as a peace deal.

Euronews also reports that Washington announced in May it would withdraw 5,000 troops from Germany and opened a six-month review of its force posture in Europe in June, with conclusions due around the end of the year. Under current rules, the Pentagon cannot drop below 76,000 soldiers in Europe in 2026 without certifying to Congress that doing so would not harm US or NATO security. The outlet judges that the defeat is unlikely to stop the gradual American drawdown from the continent.

David McAllister, a European People’s Party MEP who chairs the Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, said a shift in the balance of power does not guarantee change and that Europe must take more responsibility for its own defence.
items.cav: This is a single-outlet account drawing on anonymous EU diplomats, MEPs and an analyst, so the forecasts are opinions rather than established outcomes. Russia’s position and Zelenskyy’s silence are reported second-hand, and the article gives no vote margins and little detail on the state of the Iran conflict.
items.op: Europe should not mistake a weaker president for a safer one. Congressional checks and high veto thresholds protect anyone only when they are used openly, so European capitals should demand transparent consultation on Ukraine, Iran and troop levels. Hoping a domestic rival will do the work is not a strategy.

items.t: Stars cheer Democrats’ midterm gains, with Viola Davis, Bette Midler and John Cusack among those reacting
items.s: Celebrities have praised the Democrats after the party regained control of both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections, according to the Guardian. Many reactions came through social media posts, with some stars also marking the results at public events.
p: The Guardian reports that celebrities responded across social media and at live events after the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress. The newspaper describes the night as a string of major victories for the party, which it says reflected voter disapproval of Donald Trump and his economy.
Actor and writer John Leguizamo, who is tipped as an Oscar contender for The Odyssey, posted a video on Instagram. “This is redemption time,” he said, adding that it was “time to fix this mess.”

Bette Midler, a longtime critic of Trump, wrote that she was “OVERJOYED” and thanked America for saving what she called its beloved country. Oscar winner Viola Davis celebrated Keisha Lance Bottoms, who the Guardian says became the first Black female governor in US history, writing “CONGRATULATIONS, my sistah.”

John Cusack called for impeachment and removal, which he described as non-negotiable, and praised Abdul El-Sayed as a progressive who beat what he called a smear machine. Mark Ruffalo thanked voters for choosing decency and fairness, and Danny Trejo hailed Xavier Becerra as California’s first Latino governor.

Not all reactions were celebratory in the same way. Author Stephen King, who had hoped the enabling would stop, wrote only “Buyers’ remorse” after the results. Actor James Woods, who has previously backed Trump, mocked Republicans who he said let the outcome happen.
The Chicks celebrated on stage during a concert, declaring that Texas was blue and that both chambers were blue too. Singer Normani posted that Texas had made her proud.
items.cav: The piece relies on social media posts and a concert remark, which are reported second-hand and not independently checked. It gives no seat counts or vote margins, and phrases such as “historic” and “failing economy” are the newspaper’s and the celebrities’ own characterisations.
items.op: Celebrity applause tells us little about policy, and the coverage says nothing yet about what the new majorities will do. The real test is whether lawmakers pursue accountability in public view, with clear records and open debate. Voters who demanded transparency deserve more than slogans, and the party will ultimately be judged on what it delivers.

items.t: After the Midterms, a Weakened Trump May Press Harder on Europe, Analysts Warn
items.s: Euronews, drawing on US expert Josef Braml, argues that Democratic gains in Congress could push Donald Trump to assert himself more forcefully abroad, especially on trade and security. Europe, it says, cannot simply wait him out.
p: According to the Euronews analysis, the midterm elections curb Donald Trump’s power at home, but do not automatically make him weaker as a president. Votes were still being counted when the piece was published, yet a clear swing toward the Democrats was already visible in both chambers of Congress.

The author, citing Josef Braml, argues that a Democratic-controlled Congress can block legislation, influence budget funds, open investigations and issue subpoenas. The reasoning is that a president constrained at home has a stronger incentive to act where his room for manoeuvre is wider, namely foreign, trade and security policy.

Trade is presented as the most immediate pressure point. The piece notes that a tariff cap of 15 per cent applies to most European exports to the United States under the trade arrangement with the EU, while heavy burdens on steel and aluminium remain. It also recalls that Trump at one point raised duties on European cars and trucks to 25 per cent and tied this to demands that companies produce in the United States.

As an example, the article points to Audi, which eventually announced investments of around $4 billion for a US plant. It adds that Gernot Döllner appeared with Trump at a campaign rally in Georgia shortly before the midterms. In the author’s reading, this shows that Trump’s economic strategy relies on politically induced cost pressure rather than free trade.

On security, the piece says Europe should not expect a weaker Trump to become more compromising. It argues Washington can press European allies over Ukraine without a lengthy domestic legislative process, and that Trump has repeatedly questioned US support for NATO. It cites his renewed demand for US control over Greenland, territory belonging to NATO ally Denmark, made at the NATO summit last summer.

The Iran war is described as a further risk. More than six months after it began, the article says, there was still no lasting settlement, and the conflict showed how exposed the global economy is at the Strait of Hormuz. The author concedes it would be speculative to claim Trump will escalate for domestic reasons, but says the incentive to show toughness does not disappear with an election defeat.

The piece also points to a divided Europe as a vulnerability. It argues that Washington may cultivate bilateral ties with governments and parties hostile to Brussels, and that a fragmented EU is easier to handle than a united economic area of 450 million inhabitants.
items.cav: This is an analytical commentary built around the views of one expert, Josef Braml, and the author’s own forecasts, which the piece itself calls speculative in places. The midterm results were still being counted at publication, and the article relies on a single outlet for all its claims.
items.op: Europe should stop treating Washington’s transactional pressure as a temporary mood that an election will cure. Tariffs, alliance commitments and Ukraine policy are being used as bargaining chips, and the EU’s strongest answer is a unified, transparent position rather than bilateral deals made under duress.
